body_html:
English–Spanish cognates are words that share the same origin and look similar in both languages: family and familia, important and importante, information and información. If you know English, they are one of the biggest shortcuts in language learning. Learn a handful of spelling patterns and you can recognize, and often use, thousands of Spanish words you have never studied.

Key takeaways
  • A large share of English vocabulary has a related word in Spanish.
  • Simple ending patterns (-tion → -ción, -ty → -dad, -ly → -mente) unlock thousands of words.
  • Pronunciation differs, so say cognates the Spanish way.
  • Watch out for a small group of false friends.
{{toc}}

Why English and Spanish share so many words

Spanish grew out of Latin. English is a Germanic language, but after the Norman Conquest of 1066 it absorbed a huge number of French words, which themselves came from Latin. Later, scholars borrowed even more Latin and Greek vocabulary into English. The result is that much of the more formal, academic side of English looks remarkably like everyday Spanish.

Educators at Colorín Colorado, a bilingual education resource, often point out that 30 to 40 percent of English words have a related word in Spanish. Whatever the exact figure, the practical message is clear: you already know more Spanish than you think.

Spelling patterns for English–Spanish cognates

English endingSpanish endingExamples
-tion-ciónnation → nación, education → educación
-sion-sióndecision → decisión, television → televisión
-ty-dad / -tadcity → ciudad, liberty → libertad
-ly-menterapidly → rápidamente, finally → finalmente
-ous-oso / -osafamous → famoso, delicious → delicioso
-ic / -ical-ico / -icaromantic → romántico, music → música
-ent / -ant-ente / -antedifferent → diferente, important → importante
-ist-istaartist → artista, dentist → dentista
-ive-ivo / -ivacreative → creativo, active → activo
-ary-ario / -arianecessary → necesario, dictionary → diccionario
-al-alnatural → natural, normal → normal
{{image:2}}

Cognates by everyday topic

  • Feelings: nervioso, furioso, ansioso, optimista.
  • Home and food: el chocolate, la banana (also plátano), el tomate, la sopa (soup, careful!).
  • Health: el hospital, la medicina, el doctor, la farmacia.
  • Relationships: la familia, romántico, la pasión, la conversación.
  • Verbs: many English verbs ending in -ate become -ar verbs: celebrate → celebrar, communicate → comunicar, separate → separar.
{{book:a-road-in-bloom}}

Pronouncing cognates the Spanish way

Cognates look familiar on paper, but they sound different. Spanish vowels are short and clear, the stress often falls on a different syllable, and written accents tell you where. Hospital becomes os-pi-TAL (with a silent h); chocolate becomes cho-co-LA-te. Reading cognates aloud is a quick way to train your Spanish sounds, and it fits nicely into the routine in {{link:reading-in-spanish-for-beginners|reading in Spanish for beginners}}.

Beware of false cognates

A small group of look-alikes mean something different. Embarazada means pregnant, éxito means success and librería means bookstore. They are the exception, not the rule, but worth memorizing. I list 30 of them in {{link:spanish-false-friends|Spanish false friends}}.

{{image:3}}

How to use cognates to learn faster

  1. Hunt for them while reading. Underline every cognate on a page. You will be surprised how much of the text you already understand.
  2. Turn English words into Spanish on purpose. When you need a word, try the pattern: “responsibility” → responsabilidad. It works more often than not.
  3. Check new guesses. Look up your invented cognate once to be sure. Over time you will develop a feel for which ones work.
  4. Use them to speak sooner. Cognates let you express complex ideas early: Es una situación muy complicada.

Cognates also make it easier to find {{link:comprehensible-input-spanish|comprehensible input}}, because texts full of familiar words are understandable sooner.

Cognates in your first conversations

Cognates are especially helpful when you start speaking, because they let you say grown-up things with a small vocabulary. A few useful sentence frames:

  • Es muy importante para mí. It’s very important to me.
  • Es una idea interesante. It’s an interesting idea.
  • Es posible, pero es complicado. It’s possible, but it’s complicated.
  • Necesito más información. I need more information.
  • Tengo una pregunta personal. I have a personal question.

Mix these frames with the cognates you already know and you can hold a surprising amount of conversation in your first weeks. Native speakers will appreciate the effort, and every exchange adds new words to your memory.

A quick cognate challenge

Try reading this sentence without a dictionary: La comunicación es fundamental en una relación romántica, especialmente en situaciones difíciles. Almost every important word is a cognate: communication, fundamental, relationship, romantic, especially, situations, difficult. You just read a fairly complex Spanish sentence, and that is the quiet power of cognates.

Cognates are one of the reasons English and Spanish make such a good pair. For the whole picture, read my complete guide to {{link:bilingual-english-and-spanish|bilingual English and Spanish}}.

Partial cognates: same root, extra meanings

Some cognates overlap only partly. Discutir can mean “to discuss”, but it often means “to argue”. Realizar means “to carry out” a project, not “to realize” a fact. These partial cognates are not dangerous, just worth noticing: when a familiar word feels slightly odd in context, check whether it has a second meaning in Spanish.

Final thoughts

Cognates are a gift for anyone learning Spanish from English. Learn the patterns, say the words the Spanish way and keep an eye out for the few false friends. Every page you read will start to feel a little more like home.

faq.a: They are words with a shared origin that look and mean similar things in both languages, such as family/familia or important/importante.

faq.q: How many cognates do English and Spanish share?
faq.a: Estimates vary, but educators commonly cite that 30 to 40 percent of English words have a related Spanish word, especially more formal or academic vocabulary.

faq.q: Can I just guess Spanish words from English?
faq.a: Often, yes, using patterns like -tion to -ción. Double-check new guesses, because a small number of look-alikes are false friends.
